Base directory for this skill: /Users/michaelrihm/Documents/Projects/toolkit-v2/plugins/work/skills/work-delegate

# Work delegate

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
The only skill that makes the agent-led delivery offer and records the answer; after a yes it runs the team through the skill that owns each stage. Track these steps with the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

## Steps

1. Look for a delivery choice that covers this goal: the item's `delivery` value, its Notes > Decisions and context, and its parent's choice. A sub-item makes no offer. A quick question, a small edit, or a small item (one or two tasks, no sub-items) gets no offer: record owner-led with the reason and go on (`references/agent-led-delivery.md`, section 1).
   `toolkit work show <id> --section 'Decisions and context'`
   `toolkit work set <id> --delivery owner-led --note 'Small item: one or two tasks, so no delivery offer.'`
2. No choice recorded: add the offer as an Open Questions row, set the item waiting on the owner, and ask exactly this as the last line of the reply: "Would you like agents to take responsibility for delivering this, with you acting as product owner?" "You drive" in his own words is already the answer.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Open Questions' --append-row '| <next Q-id> | Would you like agents to take responsibility for delivering this, with you acting as product owner? | delivery | Open | owner |'`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
3. Yes: ask the team question. Where the host lets this chat list, read, and message other chats and offer new chats to the owner: "Do you want one team inside this chat, or do you want me to rename this chat to Main Orchestrator and coordinate other chats that each have their own team?" On any other host, say the multi-chat arrangement is not available here and ask: "Shall I run one team of helpers inside this chat?"
4. Main Orchestrator chosen: also ask "Do you want me to archive sessions after their task is fully complete, everything is merged and shipped, and you approved?"
5. Record the choice, the goal it covers, who said it, the date, the team arrangement, the archive answer, and the limits in Notes > Decisions and context; set the delivery value; hand the item back to the agent unless another of his questions is open; add one history note; read it back (`references/agent-led-delivery.md`, section 3).
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Decisions and context' --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --delivery agent-led`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Agent-led delivery accepted by <owner>: <his words>'`
6. No, or a later revoke: record it the same way, and set `waiting_on` to `agent` when the agent still works on the item. Do not offer again for this goal unless it grows a lot or the owner asks.
   `toolkit work set <id> --delivery owner-led`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
7. Run the team through the skill that owns each stage (`references/agent-led-delivery.md`, section 4; `references/team-arrangements.md`). The main agent plans, briefs the helpers, gives one writer per path, and is the only writer of the work item.
   `toolkit work list --tree`
8. Stop at every owner gate: set the item waiting on him and ask through the skill that owns the gate. Keep working on what the answer does not block.
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
9. Archive a chat only when its task is complete, merged and shipped, its report is saved, the owner approved it, and he said yes to archiving. Never delete a chat.
10. End every reply with the one question (the offer, the team question, or the next gate) or the exact words that continue ("Say 'go' and the team starts on P1.").

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). One-line values go in single quotes, never double quotes; an apostrophe inside them is `'\''` in Claude Code and ’ (U+2019) in Codex, or reword the text. Section text goes on standard input (`--set-file -`) in Claude Code, and in `--text '<text>'` or a `mktemp -d` file in Codex (`references/toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
- The offer and the team questions are asked word for word, in the reply text, never through a question tool.
- The `--delivery` command marks the offer's Open Questions row Answered and prints "Marked Q-xx Answered". Never edit that row by hand. When no other question for him is open, it also sets `waiting_on` to `none` ("It is no longer waiting on the owner"). Set `agent` right after it when the agent continues (steps 5 and 6); keep `owner` while another of his questions on the item is open.
- A sub-item is part of its parent's goal: creating it under the parent copies the parent's delivery value. Set it only when it is missing or differs, with a note naming the parent.
- The choice belongs to the named goal only. It does not carry over to another goal, a new item, or an unrelated sub-item.
- Acceptance alone starts no helpers; the team arrangement answer does. A no to the team question means no helpers.
- Delegation never widens merge, deployment, spending, or publishing. Every approval gate still applies, and approvals already given still count.
- Missing tracker access is not a missing decision. Keep an unsaved choice in the handoff and save it when access returns.
- A recorded lead or chat id is coordination information, not proof that an agent is still running.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Record the choice in the issue's Notes and a delivery label (`references/tracker-github.md` or `references/tracker-jira.md`).

## Agents

- `builder` (`references/agent-builder.md`), `researcher` (`references/agent-researcher.md`), and `acceptance-checker` (`references/agent-acceptance-checker.md`), briefed by the stage skill that uses them. Brief and size them as `references/helpers.md` and `references/team-roles.md` say. In Codex the main agent first makes each builder's worktree (`references/helpers.md`, section 2, "Codex builders"; Git writes: `references/git-rules.md`).
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Give the full text of this skill's `references/agent-<name>.md`, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. With no worker, do the work yourself and say that no independent check ran.

## References

| File | Open it when |
| --- | --- |
| [references/agent-led-delivery.md](references/agent-led-delivery.md) | Steps 1 to 7: when to offer, the exact questions, how to record the answers, what an acceptance allows |
| [references/team-arrangements.md](references/team-arrangements.md) | Steps 3, 7, and 9: what each team arrangement means, starting chats, archiving; also when resuming a goal with a recorded arrangement |
| [references/approvals.md](references/approvals.md) | Step 8: every owner gate still applies |
| [references/helpers.md](references/helpers.md) | Before starting any agent |
| [references/team-roles.md](references/team-roles.md) | Sizing the team |
| [references/agent-builder.md](references/agent-builder.md), [references/agent-researcher.md](references/agent-researcher.md), [references/agent-acceptance-checker.md](references/agent-acceptance-checker.md) | Codex only: the text to give the worker |
| [references/recording-owner-answers.md](references/recording-owner-answers.md) | The owner answers; history notes; `waiting_on`; a failed save |
| [references/work-item-format.md](references/work-item-format.md) | Before editing Decisions and context or Open Questions |
| [references/toolkit-commands.md](references/toolkit-commands.md) | Before a command that carries text, and on any exit code other than 0 |
| [references/git-rules.md](references/git-rules.md) | Codex: making a builder's worktree, and every Git write |
| [references/tracker-notion.md](references/tracker-notion.md) | `tracker.type` is `notion`, or a command prints a Notion error |
| [references/tracker-github.md](references/tracker-github.md) | A `toolkit work` command exits 3 in a GitHub Issues project |

1	# Planning and building a work item
2	
3	The Roadmap and Tasks formats, tracking setup, and the build rules for
4	`work-on` stages 06 to 08.
5	
6	## Contents
7	
8	1. Roadmap and tasks
9	2. The Roadmap format
10	3. The Tasks format
11	4. Status words and ticking a task
12	5. Tracking setup (stage 07)
13	6. Building (stage 08)
14	7. Keeping the item current while building
15	8. Checklist before stopping
16	
17	## 1. Roadmap and tasks
18	
19	- The Roadmap is an ordered list of phases from where the item stands to the
20	  finished result. Name phases to fit the work. "Phase" (`P1`) is the item's
21	  plan; "stage" (`08-build`) is the lifecycle. Never mix the two words.
22	- Build the phases from the approved design's "Build and verification plan"
23	  (its Technical sequence and Acceptance checks) and the chosen option's
24	  Build order. With no design (a small item that skipped design with a
25	  recorded reason), build them from the requirements.
26	- A sub-item that inherits its parent's approved design is planned from the
27	  parent's design: `toolkit work design <parent-id>`.
28	- Each phase has one or more tasks, one or more sub-items, or both.
29	- Keep detail in proportion. A one-hour fix needs one phase with one or two
30	  tasks.
31	- Link sources; do not copy them. A task names the `R-xx` it implements and
32	  the design section it follows.
33	
34	## 2. The Roadmap format
35	
36	The table keeps these columns in every tracker. The phase name follows an em
37	dash, as in the template.
38	
39	```markdown
40	A phase is complete when its tasks are complete and its exit result has been checked.
41	
42	| Phase | Outcome | Status | Exit result | Sub-items |
43	|---|---|---|---|---|
44	| P1 — CSV export button | The export button creates a file | In Progress | The file opens in Excel with every column | None. |
45	| P2 — Large exports | Exports over 10,000 rows finish | Not Started | A 50,000-row export finishes in under a minute | WI-015 |
46	```
47	
48	## 3. The Tasks format
49	
50	Each phase gets a `###` heading with the same phase id and name as its
51	Roadmap row. Each task field (`**Work:**`, `**Deliverable:**`,
52	`**Done when:**`, `**Depends on:**`) starts its own line, and every line of a
53	task but the last ends with two spaces, which Markdown reads as a line break.
54	Never run the fields together on one line.
55	
56	```markdown
57	### P1 — CSV export button
58	
59	- [ ] **P1-T01 — Add the export endpoint** · In Progress  
60	  **Work:** Add the endpoint that streams the report rows as CSV (R-01, design Technical sequence step 1).  
61	  **Deliverable:** The endpoint and its tests.  
62	  **Done when:** The endpoint test passes and a manual export opens in Excel.  
63	  **Depends on:** None.
64	- [ ] **P1-T02 — Add the Export button** · Not Started  
65	  **Work:** Add the button that calls the endpoint (R-01).  
66	  **Deliverable:** The button and its test.  
67	  **Done when:** Clicking Export downloads the file.  
68	  **Depends on:** P1-T01.
69	```
70	
71	Save both sections with the section command (`work-item-format.md`,
72	"Changing one section"):
73	
74	```text
75	toolkit work edit <id> --section Roadmap --set-file <file>
76	toolkit work edit <id> --section Tasks --set-file <file>
77	```
78	
79	## 4. Status words and ticking a task
80	
81	- Phase status: Not Started, In Progress, Done (Cancelled for a phase that
82	  was dropped). Use no other word, such as "Planned".
83	- Task status: Not Started, In Progress, Done, Cancelled.
84	- From stage 07 on, `toolkit work validate` warns when the Roadmap has no
85	  phase table, when Tasks has no checkbox lines, and when a template example
86	  row or task is left.
87	- Tick a task (`- [x]`, status Done) only with evidence: the test result
88	  line, the commit, or what the owner saw.
89	- A done or cancelled task is not reopened. Add a new task instead.
90	- A task whose "Done when" names the owner (for example "the owner confirms
91	  the wording") is not ticked by the agent. It becomes an Open Questions row
92	  with `owner` as who decides.
93	- A phase that a sub-item delivers lists the sub-item id in its Sub-items
94	  column. Finishing the sub-item does not finish or approve the parent.
95	- When the item is finished, every phase it completed says Done.
96	
97	## 5. Tracking setup (stage 07)
98	
99	Only what the item needs:
100	
101	- **Branch and worktree** for code work: the worktree
102	  `.claude/worktrees/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>` on the branch
103	  `claude/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>`, as the project's
104	  `.claude/rules/shared-repository-work.md` says. `toolkit work show <id>`
105	  prints the exact names. For WI-007:
106	  `git worktree add .claude/worktrees/wi-007-csv-export -b claude/wi-007-csv-export`
107	  In Codex this Git write needs the owner's approval and escalated
108	  permissions (`git-rules.md`).
109	- **Salesforce projects:** the item's deployment folder
110	  `delivery/deployment/<work-item-id>-<short-name>/`, copied from
111	  `delivery/deployment/work-item-deployment-template/` and kept current by
112	  `sf-component-tracker`.
113	- **A test plan**, when the checks need more than the item's acceptance
114	  checks (several scenarios, a manual check, or a release): `work-check`
115	  writes it, in `tests/` on the item's branch.
116	- **Sub-items** for phases that own real scope: open `work-organize`.
117	
118	## 6. Building (stage 08)
119	
120	- Work on the item's own branch and worktree. Never on the default branch.
121	- One task at a time, in the order the Depends on lines allow.
122	- Commit with files staged by name and a plain message. No `Co-Authored-By`
123	  line naming an AI and no "Generated with" line (`git-rules.md`).
124	- With a team recorded by `work-delegate`: one `builder` agent per
125	  independent task, each with its own files. The main agent merges each
126	  builder's branch into the item's branch, checks the tests still pass, then
127	  ticks the task. Builders never change the work item.
128	- In Codex, a builder gets no worktree by itself. Before each one starts, the
129	  main agent makes its worktree and branch and names the folder in the
130	  brief; with approvals off, one builder at a time in the item's own worktree
131	  (`helpers.md`, section 2, "Codex builders").
132	- Tests go with each task. A check that could not run is reported as not
133	  run, never as passed.
134	- Salesforce: run `sf-component-tracker` after each metadata change. Anything
135	  that changes production data goes through `sf-data-change`; agents never
136	  write production data.
137	- The build shows a requirement is wrong or missing: stop that task, add an
138	  Open Questions row, and open `work-requirements`. Do not build around it.
139	- The build shows the design does not work: record it in the design's Notes
140	  and open `solution-design` for a design change.
141	
142	## 7. Keeping the item current while building
143	
144	After each task:
145	
146	- tick it with evidence;
147	- update Overview Current position and Next action;
148	- add a history note only when something changed the plan.
149	
150	The owner may edit the record while you build. Read the section again right
151	before you change it.
152	
153	## 8. Checklist before stopping
154	
155	Before the reply that ends a session with work unfinished:
156	
157	- [ ] Overview Current position and Next action say where things stand.

# Planning and building a work item

The Roadmap and Tasks formats, tracking setup, and the build rules for
`work-on` stages 06 to 08.

## Contents

1. Roadmap and tasks
2. The Roadmap format
3. The Tasks format
4. Status words and ticking a task
5. Tracking setup (stage 07)
6. Building (stage 08)
7. Keeping the item current while building
8. Checklist before stopping

## 1. Roadmap and tasks

- The Roadmap is an ordered list of phases from where the item stands to the
  finished result. Name phases to fit the work. "Phase" (`P1`) is the item's
  plan; "stage" (`08-build`) is the lifecycle. Never mix the two words.
- Build the phases from the approved design's "Build and verification plan"
  (its Technical sequence and Acceptance checks) and the chosen option's
  Build order. With no design (a small item that skipped design with a
  recorded reason), build them from the requirements.
- A sub-item that inherits its parent's approved design is planned from the
  parent's design: `toolkit work design <parent-id>`.
- Each phase has one or more tasks, one or more sub-items, or both.
- Keep detail in proportion. A one-hour fix needs one phase with one or two
  tasks.
- Link sources; do not copy them. A task names the `R-xx` it implements and
  the design section it follows.

## 2. The Roadmap format

The table keeps these columns in every tracker. The phase name follows an em
dash, as in the template.

```markdown
A phase is complete when its tasks are complete and its exit result has been checked.

| Phase | Outcome | Status | Exit result | Sub-items |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 — CSV export button | The export button creates a file | In Progress | The file opens in Excel with every column | None. |
| P2 — Large exports | Exports over 10,000 rows finish | Not Started | A 50,000-row export finishes in under a minute | WI-015 |
```

## 3. The Tasks format

Each phase gets a `###` heading with the same phase id and name as its
Roadmap row. Each task field (`**Work:**`, `**Deliverable:**`,
`**Done when:**`, `**Depends on:**`) starts its own line, and every line of a
task but the last ends with two spaces, which Markdown reads as a line break.
Never run the fields together on one line.

```markdown
### P1 — CSV export button

- [ ] **P1-T01 — Add the export endpoint** · In Progress  
  **Work:** Add the endpoint that streams the report rows as CSV (R-01, design Technical sequence step 1).  
  **Deliverable:** The endpoint and its tests.  
  **Done when:** The endpoint test passes and a manual export opens in Excel.  
  **Depends on:** None.
- [ ] **P1-T02 — Add the Export button** · Not Started  
  **Work:** Add the button that calls the endpoint (R-01).  
  **Deliverable:** The button and its test.  
  **Done when:** Clicking Export downloads the file.  
  **Depends on:** P1-T01.
```

Save both sections with the section command (`work-item-format.md`,
"Changing one section"):

```text
toolkit work edit <id> --section Roadmap --set-file <file>
toolkit work edit <id> --section Tasks --set-file <file>
```

## 4. Status words and ticking a task

- Phase status: Not Started, In Progress, Done (Cancelled for a phase that
  was dropped). Use no other word, such as "Planned".
- Task status: Not Started, In Progress, Done, Cancelled.
- From stage 07 on, `toolkit work validate` warns when the Roadmap has no
  phase table, when Tasks has no checkbox lines, and when a template example
  row or task is left.
- Tick a task (`- [x]`, status Done) only with evidence: the test result
  line, the commit, or what the owner saw.
- A done or cancelled task is not reopened. Add a new task instead.
- A task whose "Done when" names the owner (for example "the owner confirms
  the wording") is not ticked by the agent. It becomes an Open Questions row
  with `owner` as who decides.
- A phase that a sub-item delivers lists the sub-item id in its Sub-items
  column. Finishing the sub-item does not finish or approve the parent.
- When the item is finished, every phase it completed says Done.

## 5. Tracking setup (stage 07)

Only what the item needs:

- **Branch and worktree** for code work: the worktree
  `.claude/worktrees/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>` on the branch
  `claude/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>`, as the project's
  `.claude/rules/shared-repository-work.md` says. `toolkit work show <id>`
  prints the exact names. For WI-007:
  `git worktree add .claude/worktrees/wi-007-csv-export -b claude/wi-007-csv-export`
  In Codex this Git write needs the owner's approval and escalated
  permissions (`git-rules.md`).
- **Salesforce projects:** the item's deployment folder
  `delivery/deployment/<work-item-id>-<short-name>/`, copied from
  `delivery/deployment/work-item-deployment-template/` and kept current by
  `sf-component-tracker`.
- **A test plan**, when the checks need more than the item's acceptance
  checks (several scenarios, a manual check, or a release): `work-check`
  writes it, in `tests/` on the item's branch.
- **Sub-items** for phases that own real scope: open `work-organize`.

## 6. Building (stage 08)

- Work on the item's own branch and worktree. Never on the default branch.
- One task at a time, in the order the Depends on lines allow.
- Commit with files staged by name and a plain message. No `Co-Authored-By`
  line naming an AI and no "Generated with" line (`git-rules.md`).
- With a team recorded by `work-delegate`: one `builder` agent per
  independent task, each with its own files. The main agent merges each
  builder's branch into the item's branch, checks the tests still pass, then
  ticks the task. Builders never change the work item.
- In Codex, a builder gets no worktree by itself. Before each one starts, the
  main agent makes its worktree and branch and names the folder in the
  brief; with approvals off, one builder at a time in the item's own worktree
  (`helpers.md`, section 2, "Codex builders").
- Tests go with each task. A check that could not run is reported as not
  run, never as passed.
- Salesforce: run `sf-component-tracker` after each metadata change. Anything
  that changes production data goes through `sf-data-change`; agents never
  write production data.
- The build shows a requirement is wrong or missing: stop that task, add an
  Open Questions row, and open `work-requirements`. Do not build around it.
- The build shows the design does not work: record it in the design's Notes
  and open `solution-design` for a design change.

## 7. Keeping the item current while building

After each task:

- tick it with evidence;
- update Overview Current position and Next action;
- add a history note only when something changed the plan.

The owner may edit the record while you build. Read the section again right
before you change it.

## 8. Checklist before stopping

Before the reply that ends a session with work unfinished:

- [ ] Overview Current position and Next action say where things stand.
- [ ] Notes > Resume here says exactly where to pick up.
- [ ] `waiting_on` is true: `owner` only while a question for him is open.
- [ ] One history note says what changed in this session.
- [ ] `toolkit work validate <id>` is clean.
- [ ] The current focus names the item and its real next step
      (`current-focus.md`).
- [ ] The reply ends with the one question for the owner, or the exact words
      that continue ("Say 'keep going' and I'll build P1.").

The `handoff` skill does this when the owner is clearing context.

```text
- [ ] In the right worktree, on the right branch (git branch --show-current)
- [ ] Each path staged by name
- [ ] Staged list read: only this session's files, no .work-items/ or .memory/
- [ ] Full staged diff read
- [ ] Plain message with no AI credit line
- [ ] Codex: each Git command run alone, with escalated permissions
```

Right: stage by name, read the list, commit.

```text
git add src/export.js tests/export.test.js
git diff --cached --name-status
git commit -m 'Add CSV export for invoices'
```

A small command-line tool that greets people by name. The owner named in `PROJECT.md` makes this project's decisions. The agent runs the project: it keeps the work tracker, memory, and project records current, and it does the technical work.

## Every session

- The session-start hook adds a "Project briefing" to your context: this worktree's work item, active items with the skill that continues each one, what waits on the owner, the current focus, moved items, and setup warnings. If there is no briefing, run `toolkit brief` and read it.
- Read `SOUL.md` (when the project has one) and `PROJECT.md`; read them again after resume, clear, or compaction.
- Anything to build, add, fix, or change, and "keep going": the `work-on` skill. It opens the work item; also read the item's phase in `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md`.
- A change to a requirement, such as R-01, at any stage: `work-requirements`.
- "You drive", "take it from here", "run with it", even about a named item: `work-delegate`.
- "Where are we": `work-status`. "What do you need from me" and approvals: `work-decide`.
- "Remember", "from now on", "forget that": `memory-save`. "What did we decide": `memory-find`.
- Open the matching skill or rule when the task needs its procedure. Method skills from other plugins (brainstorming, plans, debugging) may run inside these skills, never instead of them.
- Before editing files in a folder that has its own `AGENTS.md` (for example `requirements/`), read that file.
- Codex: at session start, read the always-on rules listed under "Rules".

## What the owner decides

Ask the owner and record the answer before you:
- approve requirements (build and data-load work cannot pass stage `03` without it; requirements count as approved only when the item records the owner's approval with a date; a saved draft is not approved);
- choose or approve a design, approve a finished result, or mark work Done or Cancelled;
- merge to the default branch (unless `DECISIONS.md` records a standing merge instruction), deploy, or do anything that cannot be undone;
- spend money, sign in, or change an account.

Do everything else yourself, record it, and report it. When you need a decision, add it to the work item's Open Questions with "Decision needed from: owner" and set the item's `waiting_on` to `owner` ("Work tracking" says how).

## Where information goes

| Information | Home |
| --- | --- |
| New request, idea, or bug | A new work item at stage `01-discovery` (`work-on`) |
| Requirements, questions, tasks, progress, and history of one change | That work item |
| How a change is built | `DESIGN.md` beside the item's `WORK-ITEM.md` (`toolkit work design`) |
| A decision for the whole project | `DECISIONS.md` (`work-decide`) |
| Phases and deliverable-sized work units | `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md`, naming each unit's work item ID |
| A work item's test plan | `tests/`, a copy of `TEST-PLAN-TEMPLATE.md` named for the item, committed on the item's branch; never in the tracker |
| Agreed behavior, after delivery | The area's file in `requirements/`, at stage `14-spec-update` |
| Verified structure of the current system | The area's file in `system-guide/` |
| What is in progress, owner to-dos with no work item, where the next session starts | The current focus (`memory-save`) |
| A lasting preference, correction, lesson, or hard-to-find reference | Memory (`memory-save`) |

| Outside documentation you capture | `ai-external-knowledge/`, one folder per topic |

Authorized edits to committed project documents are saved with `.claude/rules/publish-project-documents.md` and the `publish-docs` skill. Local work items and local memory are Git-ignored and never committed.

## Work tracking

- Tracker: local folders in `.work-items/`, Git-ignored, in the main checkout, shared by every worktree. `.claude/rules/work-item-folders.md` covers folders, moves, and generated files. A sub-item is an item folder nested inside its parent item's folder. It is the only tracker; never copy items into a second tracker or a local list.

## How to write replies

Claude Code applies the Plain English output style to chat. Codex and helper agents follow these lines instead.

- Start with the answer, result, or current status. Answer what was asked. Keep it short; add detail when asked.
- Use ordinary words. Explain an unfamiliar term the first time it matters. Use the exact name a system uses, the same way every time.
- Write literally: no metaphors, idioms, jokes, or picture words in place of the real name. State the point directly, without a "not this, but that" setup.
- Use paragraphs for a connected explanation, bullets for separate items or choices, and a heading only when it names what is under it.
- When asking for a decision, name the choice and the difference that matters, and recommend one.
- Use the exact status word: written, built, tested, merged, installed, or seen working. Say something works only when you saw it work.
- Leave out routine narration of process and helper activity. Give one direct line when the owner lost something, an action cannot be undone, work waits on the owner, or there is a cost.

# Work check

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Checks a finished build against every requirement with an independent checker, fixes what fails, and asks the owner to approve the result; it never merges, deploys, or marks Done. Track these steps with the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

## Steps

1. Find the item as `work-on` does: the id he named, this worktree's item, or a title that matches; two matches, ask one question naming both. Read the requirements, the Acceptance list, the Tasks, and the design's Acceptance checks; a sub-item with no design of its own is checked against its parent's (`references/testing.md`, section 1). Then set the testing stage.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit work design <id>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 09-testing`
2. Run the project's tests and every acceptance check the item lists. Several scenarios or manual steps: write a test plan in `tests/` on the item's branch (`references/testing.md`, sections 2 and 3).
3. Brief the `acceptance-checker`, never the agent that built it, naming the branch and the exact commit (`references/testing.md`, section 4).
4. Failures: run the check and fix loop until clean, or until a failure needs an owner decision (`references/testing.md`, section 5).
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 10-bug-fixing`
5. Record what was checked, the evidence, and the gaps.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Checked: <what>; evidence: <where>; gaps: <gaps or none>'`
6. Ask for the result approval with the checklist in `references/approvals.md`, section 4: stage 11, the item waiting on the owner, the result shown as "Showing the result" says below, and one question: "Do you approve this result?"
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 11-user-approval --waiting-on owner`
7. His yes: save his words first, record the approval, hand the item back to the agent, and open `work-finish`. A requirement change goes to `work-requirements`; a fix becomes a task and continues here.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner said: <quote>' --effect 'Result approved; work-finish continues.'`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --result --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
8. Update the current focus when the item's next step changed (`references/current-focus.md`). End every reply with the approval question, or the exact words that continue.

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). One-line values go in single quotes, never double quotes; an apostrophe inside them is `'\''` in Claude Code and ’ (U+2019) in Codex, or reword the text. Section text goes on standard input (`--set-file -`) in Claude Code, and in `--text '<text>'` or a `mktemp -d` file in Codex (`references/toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
- The checker is never the agent or session that built the change. When no independent check could run, say so plainly before asking for approval.
- A check that did not run is reported as not run, never as passed.
- The test plan lives in `tests/` on the item's branch, committed there. Never in `.work-items/`, which Git ignores.
- "Looks good" to any question other than the approval question is not the approval. Ask the approval question.
- Add no Open Questions row for the result approval: stage 11 already lists it as the owner's decision.
- When the approve command fails, show the owner its error. Never work around it by editing the record.
- The result approval covers the result shown, never merge, deployment, or publishing; `work-finish` handles those.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Change the stage label and record the result in the issue (`references/tracker-github.md` or `references/tracker-jira.md`).

## Showing the result

- Lead with what the result does now, in the owner's terms: "The export button now creates a CSV file that opens in Excel."
- Then how he can see it himself: the link, the command to run, or a screenshot.
- Then the evidence: tests run and their result lines, the checker's verdicts.
- Then the gaps: anything partly met, not run, or known to be missing. Never hide a gap to get an approval.
- One question: "Do you approve this result?"

A "no": record his words, turn each named problem into a task or a requirement change, and continue.

## Agents

- `acceptance-checker` (`references/agent-acceptance-checker.md`): step 3 and every re-check.
- `builder` (`references/agent-builder.md`): fixes in step 4 when a team was recorded or the owner agreed; one builder per independent fix, one writer per path. In Codex the main agent first makes each builder's worktree (`references/helpers.md`, section 2, "Codex builders").
- Brief them as `references/helpers.md` says.
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Give the full text of this skill's `references/agent-<name>.md`, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread.
